must_remember: Unpolarized light splitting into two refracted rays inside a birefringent crystal like calcite is called double refraction.
The Ordinary (O) ray obeys standard Snell's law and has a constant refractive index $\mu_o$ in all directions.
The Extraordinary (E) ray does not obey Snell's law and its velocity $v_e$ depends on the direction of propagation relative to the optic axis.
According to Huygens' wavelet theory, the O-ray produces a spherical wavefront ($v_o$), while the E-ray produces an ellipsoidal wavefront ($v_e$).
In negative uniaxial crystals like calcite, $v_e > v_o$ and $\mu_e < \mu_o$, making the sphere lie entirely inside the ellipsoid.
In positive uniaxial crystals like quartz, $v_e < v_o$ and $\mu_e > \mu_o$, making the ellipsoid lie entirely inside the sphere.
Both O-ray and E-ray are plane polarized with mutually perpendicular vibration directions.
Along the optic axis, the velocities of the O-ray and E-ray are equal, meaning double refraction does not occur in this specific direction.

glossary.meaning: The optical property of splitting a light ray into two distinct polarized rays (ordinary and extraordinary) when passing through an anisotropic medium.
The refracted ray that obeys standard Snell's law and travels with a constant velocity $v_o$ in all directions inside a birefringent crystal.
The refracted ray that does not obey Snell's law and whose velocity $v_e$ varies with the direction of propagation relative to the optic axis.
A specific direction inside a uniaxial crystal along which the velocities of the O-ray and E-ray are equal and double refraction vanishes.
A birefringent crystal in which the velocity of the extraordinary ray is greater than that of the ordinary ray ($v_e > v_o$ or $\mu_e < \mu_o$), such as calcite.
A birefringent crystal in which the velocity of the extraordinary ray is less than that of the ordinary ray ($v_e < v_o$ or $\mu_e > \mu_o$), such as quartz.
